ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Data collection was approved by the ethics committee of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences of the University of Zurich and conducted by the professional survey institute FORS (https://forscenter.ch/).
table.formatted: Data collection was approved by the ethics committee of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences of the University of Zurich and conducted by the professional survey institute FORS (<ref type="url" target="https://forscenter.ch/">https://forscenter.ch/</ref>).

table.text: Participants were invited via email to the subsequent waves.
At W1, participants were on average 50.32 years old (SD = 19.84), 50.55% were female, 40.83% had a university degree, and 83.62% held Swiss nationality.

If participants had ever volunteered, they were asked if they had volunteered in the past 6 months ("Have you volunteered for a good cause, such as by fundraising, social work, or bookkeeping for a nonprofit organization in the past 6 months?",0 = no,1 = yes).
In the following waves, participants were asked whether they had volunteered in the past 6 months (i.e., since the last assessment).

If participants had ever donated, they were asked if they had donated something in the past 6 months ("Have you donated something of value to you for charities or nonprofit organizations in the past 6 months?",0 = no,1 = yes).
In the following waves, participants were asked whether they had donated something in the past 6 months (i.e., since the last assessment).
Participants were retained if they had at least one valid personality and philanthropy observation.

> If participants had ever donated, they were asked if they had donated something in the past 6 months ("Have you donated something of value to you for charities or nonprofit organizations in the past 6 months?",0 = no,1 = yes).

> In the following waves, participants were asked whether they had donated something in the past 6 months (i.e., since the last assessment).

> Participants were retained if they had at least one valid personality and philanthropy observation.

> Data collection was approved by the ethics committee of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences of the University of Zurich and conducted by the professional survey institute FORS (https://forscenter.ch/).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .570", "p = .138", "p = .137", "p = .742" ), Sentence = c("Whereas compassion was positively associated with lifetime volunteering, OR = 1.47, 99% CI [1.35, 1.60], p < .001, politeness showed no significant association, OR = 1.02, 99% CI [0.94, 1.11], p = .570.", "Additionally, while orderliness showed no significant effect, OR = 0.94, 99% CI [0.85, 1.04], p = .138, industriousness was positively associated with later volunteering, OR = 1.11, 99% CI [1.00, 1.23], p = .007.", "While compassion positively predicted subsequent charitable giving, OR = 1.48, 99% CI [1.29, 1.69], p < .001, politeness did not, OR = 1.08, 99% CI [0.94, 1.24], p = .137.", "Similarly, industriousness was a positive predictor of charitable giving, OR = 1.16, 99% CI [1.02, 1.32], p = .003, whereas orderliness was not, OR = 0.98, 99% CI [0.86, 1.12], p = .742, and this difference was significant, b = -0.17, 99% CI [-0.32, -0.02], p = .004." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 90 columns across 10 data files.
#### Issues Identified

14 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 10 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants were invited via email to the subsequent waves.
At W1, participants were on average 50.32 years old (SD = 19.84), 50.55% were female, 40.83% had a university degree, and 83.62% held Swiss nationality.

If participants had ever volunteered, they were asked if they had volunteered in the past 6 months ("Have you volunteered for a good cause, such as by fundraising, social work, or bookkeeping for a nonprofit organization in the past 6 months?",0 = no,1 = yes).
In the following waves, participants were asked whether they had volunteered in the past 6 months (i.e., since the last assessment).

If participants had ever donated, they were asked if they had donated something in the past 6 months ("Have you donated something of value to you for charities or nonprofit organizations in the past 6 months?",0 = no,1 = yes).
In the following waves, participants were asked whether they had donated something in the past 6 months (i.e., since the last assessment).
Participants were retained if they had at least one valid personality and philanthropy observation.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 7 R code files.
#### Run order

A dependency **cycle** was detected among 2 files (03_supplementary_materials.qmd, 02_main_analyses.qmd): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—", "01_clean.qmd, 01_clean.R", 
"01_clean.qmd, 01_clean.R"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric",

#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Files the deposit does not hold

info.title: Personality Traits and Philanthropy Across Time

text.text: Philanthropic behaviors such as volunteering and charitable giving promote both societal welfare and individual well-being.

Prior research has established cross-sectional links between broad personality domains and these behaviors, but it remains open whether and how personality differences prospectively predict philanthropic engagement (selection effects) and whether such engagement may, in turn, predict personality development over time (socialization effects).
Furthermore, it is still unclear whether and how narrower personality aspects are linked to philanthropic behaviors.

Drawing on five-wave nationally representative data from Switzerland (Nwave = 2,085 to 4,475), we extend prior research by testing prospective selection effects of personality traits on later philanthropic engagement and examining socialization effects of engagement on personality trajectories across broad personality domains and their narrower aspects.
Results indicated that higher extraversion and lower neuroticism consistently predicted volunteering, whereas higher agreeableness and honesty-humility robustly predicted charitable giving.

At the lower-order level of personality aspects, meaningful differences emerged within the domains of agreeableness and conscientiousness in predicting philanthropic behaviors, with compassion and industriousness showing more consistent and positive links than politeness and orderliness.
Evidence for socialization effects was more limited.
More time spent on volunteering was associated with smaller decreases in extraversion, although this effect differed depending on the included covariates.
We discuss these findings in the context of theories on personality and prosociality and outline limitations and avenues for future research.

Understanding who engages in philanthropy and how such engagement relates to personality development could inform efforts to promote both individual well-being and societal welfare (Healy, 2002; Hui et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Understanding who engages in philanthropy and how such engagement relates to personality development could inform efforts to promote both individual well-being and societal welfare <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Healy, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Hui et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Personality traits are meaningful predictors of a wide range of life outcomes (E. D. Beck & Jackson, 2022; Ozer & Benet-Martínez, 2006; Roberts et al., 2007; Soto, 2019 Soto, , 2021)), including people's engagement in philanthropic behaviors (e.g., Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025; Stahlmann et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Personality traits are meaningful predictors of a wide range of life outcomes (E. D. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Beck & Jackson, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">Ozer & Benet-Martínez, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">Roberts et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b161">Soto, 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b162">Soto, , 2021))</ref>, including people's engagement in philanthropic behaviors (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b165">Stahlmann et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Volunteering and charitable giving are core examples of such philanthropic engagement (Bekkers, 2006 (Bekkers, , 2010)).
text.formatted: Volunteering and charitable giving are core examples of such philanthropic engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Bekkers, 2006</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Bekkers, , 2010))</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analytic evidence indicates that high levels of extraversion and openness are linked to volunteering, whereas high levels of agreeableness are related to charitable giving (Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic evidence indicates that high levels of extraversion and openness are linked to volunteering, whereas high levels of agreeableness are related to charitable giving <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, effect sizes vary considerably across studies.
This heterogeneity may stem from over-reliance on small samples and brief personality inventories, which limits precision and the ability to examine broad and narrow personality traits.

Notably, theory and preliminary evidence suggest that narrow personality traits (e.g., compassion vs. politeness aspects of agreeableness) may differ in their relation to philanthropic behaviors (Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025; Smillie et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2017b), implying that associations observed at the broad domain level may be obscured or imprecise (Stahlmann et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Notably, theory and preliminary evidence suggest that narrow personality traits (e.g., compassion vs. politeness aspects of agreeableness) may differ in their relation to philanthropic behaviors <ref type="bibr">(Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">Smillie et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b196">Zhao et al., 2017b)</ref>, implying that associations observed at the broad domain level may be obscured or imprecise <ref type="bibr" target="#b164">(Stahlmann et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, most existing research has relied on cross-sectional data and predominantly focused on concurrent links between personality traits and current or lifetime prevalence of philanthropic engagement.

Longitudinal research examining both prospective selection effects of personality traits on subsequent philanthropic behavior and potential socialization effects of philanthropic participation on personality development remains scarce (cf.
Luengo Kanacri et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Luengo <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Kanacri et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, personalityphilanthropy transactions may unfold differently across the lifespan, raising the possibility of unique age-dependent links between personality traits and philanthropic behaviors.
The present study extends previous research by examining the longitudinal transactions between philanthropic behaviors and both broad and narrow personality traits across the lifespan.
We used data from a nationally representative sample of Swiss adults who participated in a 5-wave longitudinal study spanning 2 years.

By integrating repeated assessments of volunteering, charitable giving, and personality traits, we distinguished cross-sectional associations from prospective selection and socialization effects and tested how lower-order traits may have unique, developmentally sensitive links with philanthropic engagement beyond broader personality domains.

Volunteering and charitable giving are common forms of civic engagement often referred to as traditional philanthropy 1 (distinguished from health-related philanthropy such as blood donation; Bekkers, 2006 Bekkers, , 2010)).

text.text: They involve donating time, effort, money, or other goods to individuals or organizations outside one's family and friends (Penner, 2002) 2 .

text.text: Taken together, meta-analytic findings suggest that being engaged in volunteering and, to a lesser degree, charitable giving is associated with adaptive levels of higher-order personality traits (Bleidorn, Hopwood, Ackerman, et al., 2020; Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025; Marsh et al., 2022; Yelbuz & Thielmann, 2024).

text.text: Volunteering has been related to higher extraversion, openness/intellect, conscientiousness, honesty-humility, and lower neuroticism, whereas charitable giving correlates with higher levels of agreeableness, conscientiousness, and honesty-humility.
Although these effect sizes tend to be small, their practical implications can be substantial at the population level (Funder & Ozer, 2019; Götz et al., 2022; Ozer & Benet-Martínez, 2006).

text.text: For instance, even an association as small as r ≈ .05 could scale up to sizable differences in philanthropic behaviors over time when leveraged through personality-tailored recruitment of volunteers (Hirsh et al., 2012).

text.text: However, such reasoning presupposes that effect sizes are estimated reliably.

Prior research may have fallen short in this regard: theoretical expectations and empirical findings sometimes diverge, as illustrated by the attenuation of the agreeableness-volunteering link after correcting for small-study effects (Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Prior research may have fallen short in this regard: theoretical expectations and empirical findings sometimes diverge, as illustrated by the attenuation of the agreeableness-volunteering link after correcting for small-study effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: More extensive personality measures that distinguish both broad domains and lower-order aspects, administered in sufficiently large and representative samples, are therefore essential for producing precise and stable estimates.
Moreover, existing research focused on concurrent links, providing limited insights into how personality and philanthropy relate to one another over time.

Personality traits and philanthropic behaviors could be linked because people with certain trait levels are more likely to later engage in volunteering or charitable giving (selection effects) or because personality traits change in response to engagement in philanthropic behaviors (socialization effects).
Social selection refers to the tendency for people with certain traits to end up in social environments and roles that align with those traits (Caspi et al., 2005; Roberts & Jackson, 2008).
text.formatted: Social selection refers to the tendency for people with certain traits to end up in social environments and roles that align with those traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Caspi et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">Roberts & Jackson, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with previous research (e.g., Bühler et al., 2022 Bühler et al., , 2024;; Wrzus & Neyer, 2016), we use the term selection broadly to capture processes that guide people with certain individual characteristics towards specific events, contexts, or behaviors.
text.formatted: Consistent with previous research (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Bühler et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Bühler et al., , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b184">Wrzus & Neyer, 2016)</ref>, we use the term selection broadly to capture processes that guide people with certain individual characteristics towards specific events, contexts, or behaviors.

text.text: In this sense, relatively stable personality traits have been theorized and found to predict later life outcomes, such as childbirth, occupational choices, and divorce (E. D. Beck & Jackson, 2022; Ozer & Benet-Martínez, 2006; Roberts et al., 2007).
text.formatted: In this sense, relatively stable personality traits have been theorized and found to predict later life outcomes, such as childbirth, occupational choices, and divorce (E. D. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Beck & Jackson, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">Ozer & Benet-Martínez, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">Roberts et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: One important mechanism of selection is niche-picking, whereby individuals actively choose, shape, and maintain environments that fit their personal needs and preferences (Roberts & Damian, 2019).
text.formatted: One important mechanism of selection is niche-picking, whereby individuals actively choose, shape, and maintain environments that fit their personal needs and preferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">(Roberts & Damian, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For example, extraverted people may decide to volunteer because they expect opportunities to socialize with other people.
However, selection can also occur less actively, when differences in personality traits shape how individuals perceive, interpret, or are exposed to opportunities for philanthropy.
For instance, agreeable individuals may notice and thus seize more opportunities to donate to charitable causes, because they are particularly attuned to others' needs.

The cross-sectional associations reviewed above provide an initial empirical basis for theorizing about selection effects from specific personality traits on different forms of philanthropic engagement.

Because personality traits have long been theorized to be relatively stable across adulthood, they have often been examined as predictors distinguishing individuals who are more or less likely to engage in philanthropic behaviors, even if these variables were assessed simultaneously (e.g., Ackermann, 2019; King et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Because personality traits have long been theorized to be relatively stable across adulthood, they have often been examined as predictors distinguishing individuals who are more or less likely to engage in philanthropic behaviors, even if these variables were assessed simultaneously (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Ackermann, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">King et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, two main problems prevent causal conclusions.
First, cross-sectional data cannot establish whether personality differences precede philanthropic engagement or simply co-occur with it.
Consequently, prospective selection effects can differ from cross-sectional patterns.

For example, agreeableness may correlate with charitable giving at baseline because prior donors have become more agreeable, yet baseline agreeableness may not predict new donations among previously uninvolved individuals (cf. Caprara et al., 2012).
text.formatted: For example, agreeableness may correlate with charitable giving at baseline because prior donors have become more agreeable, yet baseline agreeableness may not predict new donations among previously uninvolved individuals (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Caprara et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Prospective analyses are therefore essential to account for temporal precedence and test which personality traits forecast later philanthropic engagement.
Second, third variables may confound the relationship between personality traits and philanthropy.

Economic resources, for example, have been linked to both personality traits such as openness/intellect, conscientiousness, and extraversion (e.g., Vella, 2024) and charitable donations (e.g., Schulreich et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Economic resources, for example, have been linked to both personality traits such as openness/intellect, conscientiousness, and extraversion (e.g., Vella, 2024) and charitable donations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b157">Schulreich et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Confounding of between-person differences in these variables can be addressed by statistically controlling for them and may be reduced by adopting longitudinal designs that isolate differences in trait levels and trait change trajectories.

However, time-varying withinperson confounders remain a threat to causal inference and demand clear articulation of underlying assumptions in psychological fields where experimental designs are not feasible (Grosz et al., 2020; Rohrer, 2018).
text.formatted: However, time-varying withinperson confounders remain a threat to causal inference and demand clear articulation of underlying assumptions in psychological fields where experimental designs are not feasible <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Grosz et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">Rohrer, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This limitation applies to both directional interpretations: that personality traits shape philanthropic engagement and that philanthropic engagement contributes to personality change.
Longitudinal data also enable tests of this latter pathway of socialization, whereby engaging in philanthropic behaviors may be linked to personality development over time.

Across adulthood, individuals tend to show adaptive personality change by becoming more agreeable, conscientious, and emotionally stable on average (e.g., Bleidorn et al., 2019; Bleidorn, Hopwood, Ackerman, et al., 2020; Roberts, Walton, et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Across adulthood, individuals tend to show adaptive personality change by becoming more agreeable, conscientious, and emotionally stable on average (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Bleidorn et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Bleidorn, Hopwood, Ackerman, et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">Roberts, Walton, et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Social investment theory proposes that such normative development results from investing in social roles that demand caring, reliable, and emotionally regulated behavior (Roberts et al., 2005; Roberts & Nickel, 2017).
text.formatted: Social investment theory proposes that such normative development results from investing in social roles that demand caring, reliable, and emotionally regulated behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">(Roberts et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b152">Roberts & Nickel, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: As individuals commit to role-related responsibilities, they adapt their patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, and these adaptations may gradually consolidate into enduring traits.

Consistent with this idea, socialization effects tend to be stronger when psychological role investment is high (Lodi-Smith & Roberts, 2007), although empirical support is overall mixed and effect sizes tend to be smaller than for selection effects (Bleidorn et al., 2013; Bühler et al., 2022 Bühler et al., , 2024;; Den Boer et al., 2019; Haehner, Krämer, Wright, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Consistent with this idea, socialization effects tend to be stronger when psychological role investment is high <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Lodi-Smith & Roberts, 2007)</ref>, although empirical support is overall mixed and effect sizes tend to be smaller than for selection effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Bleidorn et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Bühler et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Bühler et al., , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Den Boer et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Haehner, Krämer, Wright, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Philanthropic engagement may elicit socialization effects in line with social investment theory.

Such behaviors can function as social roles when they involve sustained, normatively valued commitments that integrate individuals into broader social systems and foster a sense of affective, cognitive, and behavioral investment in the role (Bekkers, 2006; Lodi-Smith & Roberts, 2007).
text.formatted: Such behaviors can function as social roles when they involve sustained, normatively valued commitments that integrate individuals into broader social systems and foster a sense of affective, cognitive, and behavioral investment in the role <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Bekkers, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">Lodi-Smith & Roberts, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Especially volunteering has been theorized to constitute a social role (Penner, 2002).
text.formatted: Especially volunteering has been theorized to constitute a social role <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">(Penner, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: In line with social investment theory, the decisive question may, however, not be whether someone engages in volunteering or not but how much a person invests in this social role.

Investing more time in volunteering may thus be associated with specific personality trait changes that align with that role, such as becoming more extraverted through frequent social engagement and more open through repeated exposure to unfamiliar, intellectually stimulating contexts.
In contrast, charitable giving generally involves less psychological role commitment (Bekkers & Wiepking, 2011).
text.formatted: In contrast, charitable giving generally involves less psychological role commitment <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Bekkers & Wiepking, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Again, simple lifetime prevalence of having ever donated may not be consequential for personality development.

Moreover, even individuals who regularly donate money may not necessarily identify with their role as a donor; they may simply view donating as a straightforward use of surplus income or as a way to feel good about themselves and fulfill a perceived moral responsibility.

If charitable giving affects personality at all, such effects may operate mainly cognitively: as people reflect on their prosocial actions, they may view themselves as more caring or dutiful, potentially elevating self-reports of agreeableness or conscientiousness with higher amounts donated (for socialization effects of general prosociality on these traits, see Caprara et al., 2012; Luengo Kanacri et al., 2014).
text.formatted: If charitable giving affects personality at all, such effects may operate mainly cognitively: as people reflect on their prosocial actions, they may view themselves as more caring or dutiful, potentially elevating self-reports of agreeableness or conscientiousness with higher amounts donated (for socialization effects of general prosociality on these traits, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Caprara et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Luengo Kanacri et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, these dynamics are unlikely to produce profound personality changes in habitual patterns of feelings and behaviors, and we therefore treated socialization effects of charitable giving on personality change exploratorily.

Because role demands of philanthropic activities map more directly onto concrete behavioral tendencies, narrower personality aspects-such as assertiveness, compassion, or openness-may be specifically sensitive to socialization.

These aspects can also show distinct developmental trajectories within the same domain (Haehner, Krämer, Schaefer, et al., 2026), implying that different mechanisms may shape different aspects over time.
text.formatted: These aspects can also show distinct developmental trajectories within the same domain <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Haehner, Krämer, Schaefer, et al., 2026)</ref>, implying that different mechanisms may shape different aspects over time.

text.text: Together, both the specificity of role demands and the heterogeneity of aspect-level development underscore the value of examining socialization effects also at the level of lower-order traits.
The effects of both selection and socialization processes for philanthropic behaviors may wax and wane across the lifespan.
Lifespan theories highlight age-graded changes in goals, resources, and social roles (Erikson, 1994; Freund & Baltes, 2002).
text.formatted: Lifespan theories highlight age-graded changes in goals, resources, and social roles <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Erikson, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Freund & Baltes, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Prosocial motives and values such as generativity, altruism, and self-transcendence tend to become more salient with higher age (Freund & Blanchard-Fields, 2014; McAdams, 2001), and philanthropic behaviors such as volunteering and charitable giving are more prevalent in middle and later adulthood (Best & Freund, 2021; Mayr & Freund, 2020; Shane et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Prosocial motives and values such as generativity, altruism, and self-transcendence tend to become more salient with higher age <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Freund & Blanchard-Fields, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">McAdams, 2001)</ref>, and philanthropic behaviors such as volunteering and charitable giving are more prevalent in middle and later adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Best & Freund, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">Mayr & Freund, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b159">Shane et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Personal resources-such as leisure time, income, or social networks-also change systematically across the lifespan, potentially amplifying or constraining opportunities for philanthropic engagement.
Together, such age-graded shifts make it plausible that both selection and socialization processes differ across age.
For personality-based selection effects, there are theoretical arguments supporting either direction of age moderation.

When life paths are still relatively open in young adulthood and philanthropic activities are less normative, the effect of personality traits on niche-picking may be amplified, because only individuals strongly predisposed to philanthropy might engage in philanthropic behavior.

At the same time, with increasing age-when life structures stabilize and competing role demands decline (e.g., after retirement; Hämäläinen et al., 2024)-individuals also tend to gain more freedom to choose prosocial roles aligned with their personality traits, potentially strengthening selection processes.
text.formatted: At the same time, with increasing age-when life structures stabilize and competing role demands decline (e.g., after retirement; <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Hämäläinen et al., 2024)</ref>-individuals also tend to gain more freedom to choose prosocial roles aligned with their personality traits, potentially strengthening selection processes.

text.text: It is thus unclear whether higher age promotes or reduces the predictive power of personality traits on philanthropic engagement.
Similarly, socialization effects may either weaken or strengthen with age.
Philanthropy-related role experiences may exert larger effects on personality earlier in adulthood when traits are more malleable (Bleidorn et al., 2022; Roberts, Walton, et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Philanthropy-related role experiences may exert larger effects on personality earlier in adulthood when traits are more malleable <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">Roberts, Walton, et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, as prosocial roles become more normative, identity-defining, and institutionally embedded with age, this could deepen psychological investment and, in turn, increase the potential for role-related personality change (Lodi-Smith & Roberts, 2007; Neyer et al., 2014).
text.formatted: In contrast, as prosocial roles become more normative, identity-defining, and institutionally embedded with age, this could deepen psychological investment and, in turn, increase the potential for role-related personality change <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Lodi-Smith & Roberts, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Neyer et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, insofar as selection and socialization processes are conceptually linked (Roberts & Nickel, 2017), age-related conditions that shape one process may plausibly shape the other as well.
text.formatted: Moreover, insofar as selection and socialization processes are conceptually linked <ref type="bibr" target="#b152">(Roberts & Nickel, 2017)</ref>, age-related conditions that shape one process may plausibly shape the other as well.

text.text: However, whether age amplifies or attenuates socialization effects remains unclear.

In this study, we addressed limitations of previous research on Big Five and honesty-humility personality traits and philanthropic engagement by examining links between lower-order aspects and real-life philanthropy across 2 years in a representative sample.
We distinguished concurrent associations, prospective selection effects, and socialization links in three main research questions to gain a comprehensive understanding (see Table 1).

text.text: Research Questions About the Relationships Between Personality and Philanthropy 1: Are personality traits concurrently associated with lifetime prevalence of volunteering and charitable giving?
1a: Do associations differ between trait aspects within domains?
1b (exploratory): Are associations moderated by age?
2: Do personality traits prospectively predict volunteering and charitable giving?
2a: Do prospective selection effects differ between trait aspects within domains?
2b (exploratory): Are selection effects moderated by age?
3: Do volunteering and charitable giving affect personality traits over time?
3a: Do socialization effects differ between trait aspects within domains?
3b (exploratory): Are socialization effects moderated by age?

text.text: Across research 336 questions, we tested honesty-humility, all Big Five trait domains and their 10 aspects although we did 337 not have confirmatory hypotheses regarding conscientiousness and neuroticism.
338 Prospective selection effects were tested using binary indicators of philanthropic behaviors, representing selection into or continuation of volunteering/charitable giving.
Socialization effects were tested using continuous measures of philanthropic engagement, representing the number of hours volunteered and the amount of money donated, respectively.

This distinction reflects two complementary processes: selection concerns whether personality predicts who engages in philanthropic behaviors at all, whereas socialization concerns whether the extent of such engagement is associated with personality change.

As additional robustness tests, we also conducted prospective selection analyses using continuous measures of philanthropic engagement and socialization analyses using binary indicators of philanthropy.
These supplementary analyses are reported in Sections 3 and 4 of the Supplementary Materials.

Regarding Research Questions 1a, 2a, and 3a, we hypothesized personality aspects within the same domain would show differential associations with philanthropic behaviors, without specifying the direction or magnitude of these differences (Hypothesis 4).

Given that the same age-graded conditions can plausibly strengthen or weaken both selection and socialization processes, and empirical evidence is limited and mixed (Bühler et al., 2024; Denissen et al., 2019; Wrzus, 2019), there is no clear basis for a directional prediction of age moderation.

text.text: Accordingly, we examined Research Questions 1b, 2b, and 3b exploratorily.

text.text: We used data from the PERCIVAL project, a 2-year longitudinal study conducted in Switzerland and funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation (Grant number 205026).
Five assessment waves (W1 to W5) were evenly spread between September 2022 and September 2024.
Data collection was approved by the ethics committee of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences of the University of Zurich and conducted by the professional survey institute FORS (https://forscenter.ch/).
text.formatted: Data collection was approved by the ethics committee of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences of the University of Zurich and conducted by the professional survey institute FORS (<ref type="url" target="https://forscenter.ch/">https://forscenter.ch/</ref>).

text.text: The sample was drawn from the sampling frame for surveys of persons and households of the Swiss Federal Statistical Office.
A probability sample (N = 16,052) of adult Swiss residents was invited to take part in the study.

The sample was stratified based on gender (female, male), three age groups (18-34 years, 35-64 years, 65+ years), and the seven major Swiss regions (Lake Geneva Region, Espace Mittelland, Northwestern Switzerland, Zurich, Eastern Switzerland, Central Switzerland, Ticino;
Federal Office for Spatial Development, 1999).
Participants were invited via email to the subsequent waves.
In the present study, we used data from participants who completed the W1 survey (N = 4,529).
To ensure high data quality, we excluded data from n = 54 participants who provided the same response to more than 15 consecutive personality trait items (Yentes & Wilhelm, 2023).
text.formatted: To ensure high data quality, we excluded data from n = 54 participants who provided the same response to more than 15 consecutive personality trait items <ref type="bibr" target="#b192">(Yentes & Wilhelm, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The final sample sizes were NW1 = 4,475, NW2 = 2,462, NW3 = 2,555, NW4 = 2,085, and NW5 = 2,360.
At W1, participants were on average 50.32 years old (SD = 19.84), 50.55% were female, 40.83% had a university degree, and 83.62% held Swiss nationality.

Attrition analyses indicated that participants who dropped out after W1 were more likely male, younger, more neurotic, less agreeable, less open/intellectual, and less often volunteers and donors (p < .01).

text.text: The effect sizes of these group differences were small, with the biggest effect size being d = 0.22 for agreeableness.
Details on attrition analyses can be found in Section 1.1 of the Supplementary Materials.
Big Five personality domains and aspects were assessed with the Big Five Aspect Scales (BFAS; DeYoung et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Big Five personality domains and aspects were assessed with the Big Five Aspect Scales <ref type="bibr">(BFAS;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">DeYoung et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The BFAS consist of 100 items capturing the Big Five domains with two lower-order aspects each: neuroticism (volatility and withdrawal), agreeableness (compassion and politeness), conscientiousness (industriousness and orderliness), extraversion (enthusiasm and assertiveness), and openness/intellect (intellect and openness).
Items were assessed on a 5-point scale from1 = strongly disagree to5 = strongly agree (e.g., "take charge" = assertiveness, or "waste my time" = industriousness reverse coded).
The full 100-item BFAS was used at W1 and W2.
To reduce participant burden in the following waves, a 40-item short version of the BFAS was used (BFAS-40; Gallagher et al., 2023).
text.formatted: To reduce participant burden in the following waves, a 40-item short version of the BFAS was used (BFAS-40; <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Gallagher et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: German, French, and Italian translations of the BFAS and BFAS-40 have been validated in the PERCIVAL sample (Haehner et al., 2025).

text.text: Both scale versions showed satisfactory convergence and acceptable psychometric properties in terms of their factorial validity and reliability.

Internal consistencies ranged from w = .83 to .91 for domains and w = .69 to .87 for aspects (long form) and w = .69 to .81 for domains and w = .51 to .75 for aspects (short form) at W1 in this sample.
We calculated mean scores for the Big Five domains and 10 aspects and z-standardized them prior to analysis.

HEXACO honesty-humility was assessed at W2 and W5 with the 10-item honesty-humility subscale of the 60-item version of the HEXACO Personality Inventory (HEXACO-60; Ashton & Lee, 2009; Lee & Ashton, 2004).

In contrast to the analyses with Big Five traits, we did not conduct separate analyses for lower-order facets of honestyhumility (sincerity, fairness, greed-avoidance, modesty).
These facets were assessed with only 2 to 3 items and are not recommended for use as mean scores in this short instrument (Ashton & Lee, 2009).

We calculated mean scores and z-standardized them prior to analysis.

At W1, participants reported whether they had ever volunteered ("Have you ever volunteered for a good cause, such as by fundraising, social work, or bookkeeping for a nonprofit organization?",0 = no,1 = yes).

If participants had ever volunteered, they were asked if they had volunteered in the past 6 months ("Have you volunteered for a good cause, such as by fundraising, social work, or bookkeeping for a nonprofit organization in the past 6 months?",0 = no,1 = yes).
In the following waves, participants were asked whether they had volunteered in the past 6 months (i.e., since the last assessment).

Participants who volunteered in the past 6 months were asked to indicate the cause(s) they volunteered for (multiple choice; sport/recreation/hobby, welfare/community, health, emergency services, education/training/youth development, religion, environment, business/professional/union, law/justice/politics, arts/culture, foreign/international, other).
At W1 and W2, participants who reported volunteering in the past 6 months indicated how many hours per month they typically volunteered (open numeric entry).
We checked these entries, excluded negative values, and harmonized any range or non-numeric entries (e.g., "around 6 to 7 hours" was coded as 6.5 hours).
As preregistered, we winsorized these numeric entries to 45 hours to reduce the influence of extreme values.
At W3-W5, volunteering hours were assessed using an ordinal scale with 10 categories ("less than 1 hour per month" to "more than 40 hours per month").
For analyses, we assigned midpoints to all categories; for the top category we used 45 hours to be consistent across waves.
Numeric and categorical values were then combined to a quasi-continuous measure of monthly volunteering hours in the past 6 months.
Because this variable was strongly skewed (skewness = 1.74), we applied log-transformation prior to z-standardization.

At W1, participants reported whether they had ever donated something of value ("Have you ever donated something of value to you for charities or nonprofit organizations, such as money, food, or clothes?",0 = no,1 = yes).

If participants had ever donated, they were asked if they had donated something in the past 6 months ("Have you donated something of value to you for charities or nonprofit organizations in the past 6 months?",0 = no,1 = yes).
In the following waves, participants were asked whether they had donated something in the past 6 months (i.e., since the last assessment).
Participants who reported donations in the past six months were asked to indicate the type(s) of donations they made (multiple choice; money, food, clothes, furniture, electrical items, other).
At W1 and W2, participants who reported donating money indicated how much they had donated in the past 6 months (open numeric entry, in CHF).
We checked these entries, excluded negative values, and harmonized any range or non-numeric entries (e.g., "maybe 100 or 150 francs" was coded as CHF 125).
We winsorized these numeric entries exceeding mean + 3 SD.
At W3-W5, the amount of monetary donations was assessed using an ordinal response scale with 11 categories ("CHF 1-100" to "more than CHF 1,000").
We assigned midpoints to all categories; for the top category, we used CHF 1,500 as estimate, reflecting plausible variation above CHF 1,000.
Numeric and categorical values were combined to a quasi-continuous measure of monetary donations in the past 6 months.
Because the resulting distribution was strongly skewed (skewness = 9.70), we applied log-transformation prior to z-standardization.
Age (in years) was computed based on participants' birth year at W1 in 2022.
We grand-mean centered this variable across participants to ease interpretation.
Average monthly net income was assessed at W1 in 16 exhaustive income brackets ("Less than CHF 1,000" to "More than CHF 15,000").
At W3 and W5, individuals indicated whether their income had changed in the past 12 months.
If their income had changed, they were asked to specify their current income.
Each bracket was represented by its midpoint (the top bracket by CHF 15,500) to obtain a quasi-continuous income variable.
We averaged across available waves within participants to get a time-invariant income control variable.
Because the distribution was strongly skewed (skewness = 1.60), we applied logtransformation prior to z-standardization.
Analyses were conducted in R (version 4.5.2) using the package lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) and its extension lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017) for main analyses.

text.text: Extended models additionally included a) age as a moderator and b) income as a control variable for between-person differences in economic resources and provided exploratory tests of age moderation effects (RQ1b, RQ2b, RQ3b).
Individuals with no valid income entry only contributed to main but not to extended models.

Group comparisons indicated that individuals who reported their income (n = 3,101) were more likely male, showed higher levels of extraversion, conscientiousness, openness/intellect, lower levels of neuroticism, and were more likely to have ever donated money compared to individuals who did not report their income (n = 1,374), with effect sizes of |d| = 0.13-0.26.
The sample size and composition thus differed substantially between main and extended models (see Section 1.2 of the Supplementary Materials).
We therefore expanded the preregistered analyses by additionally fitting extended models without income as a control variable.
This allowed us to examine age moderation both in the income-complete subsample and the full sample (without income control).
Details on these extended analyses are reported in the Supplementary Materials (Sections 2-4).

To examine cross-sectional associations between personality traits and lifetime prevalence of philanthropic engagement, we estimated logistic regression models to predict lifetime prevalence of volunteering and charitable giving at W1 (binary;0 = never engaged before W1,1 = engaged before W1) with concurrently assessed personality traits 4 .
Separate models were fitted for each philanthropic behavior and for each personality domain and aspect, respectively.
For these cross-sectional analyses, we focused on W1 as it provided the largest sample size and included the full 100-item BFAS.
Missing data were handled by using listwise deletion, including all cases with observed predictor and outcome values.

To examine whether engaging in philanthropy was associated with changes in personality traits over time, we estimated multilevel linear models with repeated observations (waves; Level 1) nested within individuals (Level 2).

We examined whether age moderated cross-sectional associations, prospective selection, and socialization effects.
Full results on age moderation are reported in Sections 2.4.2 (RQ1), 3.4.2 (RQ2), and 4.4.2 (RQ3) of the Supplementary Materials.
Overall, only a few age moderation effects were significant; these effects were very small (0.99 ≤ OR ≤ 1.01 and |b| ≤ 0.01) and scattered across main and supplemental analyses.

Significant age moderation effects (without controlling for income) mostly emerged for agreeableness and its aspect compassion, specifically for concurrent associations with charitable giving as well as prospective selection into volunteering and amount of money donated.
These positive links tended to be slightly stronger with increasing age.

Additionally, assertiveness was more strongly related to lifetime volunteering among older compared to younger adults, and the non-significant socialization links between average volunteering hours and change in enthusiasm as well as honestyhumility became increasingly negative with age.
Beyond these findings, no consistent age moderation patterns were observed.
Finally, we conducted all analyses while additionally controlling for income (see Sections 2, 3, and 4 of the Supplementary Materials).

Even though the sample size and sample composition deviated substantially from our main analyses (DNW1 = 1,374; see Section 1.2 of the Supplementary Materials), most of the confirmatory effects remained significant in the models controlling for income.

Exceptions were the concurrent link of honesty-humility with volunteering, the prospective selection effects of openness/intellect on volunteering, and the socialization effect on extraversion, which were not significant in this income-controlled model specification.
In contrast, most age moderation effects reported above did not hold once income was controlled.

Only the age moderation of the prospective effects of compassion (on volunteering participation and the amount of money donated) and of the socialization effect of volunteering hours on honesty-humility remained significant.

Conversely, additional moderation effects emerged specifically in the income-controlled models: the prospective effects of agreeableness and compassion on hours volunteered were stronger at older ages, whereas the prospective effect of politeness on charitable giving was somewhat weaker.
Thus, most age moderation effects were not robust.
Volunteering and charitable giving constitute core forms of philanthropic engagement with beneficial effects for recipients, donors, and broader societal functioning.

This study extends prior research by moving beyond established concurrent links to examine prospective selection and socialization associations between broad and narrow personality traits and philanthropy in five-wave longitudinal data from a nationally representative sample of Switzerland.
There were three major findings in this study.
First, extraversion and neuroticism consistently predicted volunteering, whereas agreeableness and honesty-humility emerged as robust predictors of charitable giving.

Second, at the lower-order aspect level, meaningful differences emerged within the domains of agreeableness and conscientiousness: compassion and industriousness showed more consistent and positive links with philanthropic behavior than politeness and orderliness.
Third, evidence for socialization was more limited, with only one effect: people who spent more time volunteering tended to show more stable extraversion trajectories.
Age rarely moderated these associations, suggesting largely similar patterns across the adult lifespan.
In the following, we discuss cross-sectional associations before turning to longitudinal evidence of selection and socialization processes and the broader context and implications of this study.
Overall, we found broad evidence for links between lifetime prevalence of philanthropic behaviors and personality traits at both the domain and aspect level.

Both aspects of extraversion were positively associated with lifetime volunteering and charitable giving, suggesting that sociable and agentic people were more likely to have ever volunteered or donated to charity.
Agreeableness and compassion were linked to both having volunteered and donated, whereas politeness was only related to lifetime charitable giving.
Conscientiousness was also positively associated with lifetime charitable giving, whereas orderliness, unlike industriousness, was negatively associated with lifetime volunteering.
Openness/intellect and both its aspects were positively associated with lifetime volunteering and charitable giving.
In contrast, neuroticism and both withdrawal and volatility were negatively associated with both philanthropic behaviors.
Finally, honesty-humility was positively associated with lifetime volunteering and charitable giving.

Consistent with prior meta-analytic effect sizes for the Big Five (Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025), hypothesized associations of extraversion and openness/intellect with volunteering were very small to small (OR = 1.39-1.45, r ≈ .09-.10 9 ) and the concurrent link between agreeableness and charitable giving was small to medium (OR = 1.73, r ≈ .15).

text.text: Similarly, we found a very small association between honesty-humility and volunteering (OR = 1.18, r ≈ .05) and a small association between this trait and charitable giving (OR = 1.53, r ≈ .12).

These associations were considerably weaker than prior single-study estimates (Marsh et al., 2022; Yelbuz & Thielmann, 2024) as well as meta-analytic evidence from prosocial behavior in the lab (Thielmann et al., 2020; Zettler et al., 2020).
text.formatted: These associations were considerably weaker than prior single-study estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Marsh et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b191">Yelbuz & Thielmann, 2024)</ref> as well as meta-analytic evidence from prosocial behavior in the lab <ref type="bibr" target="#b171">(Thielmann et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b194">Zettler et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Despite their limited effect size, these associations should not be dismissed as irrelevant: in complex real-life behaviors like volunteering and charitable giving, which are shaped by many factors, effects of this magnitude are theoretically expected and can yield meaningful practical implications when aggregated across many people and opportunities for prosocial action (Funder & Ozer, 2019; Götz et al., 2022; Ozer & Benet-Martínez, 2006).

text.text: We elaborate on these implications further below.

Whereas earlier research has often emphasized agreeableness and honesty-humility as key correlates of philanthropic activities (Bekkers, 2006; Carlo et al., 2005; Smillie et al., 2019), our findings suggest a broader and more nuanced range of relevant traits that distinguish engaged from non-engaged people.
text.formatted: Whereas earlier research has often emphasized agreeableness and honesty-humility as key correlates of philanthropic activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Bekkers, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Carlo et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">Smillie et al., 2019)</ref>, our findings suggest a broader and more nuanced range of relevant traits that distinguish engaged from non-engaged people.

text.text: Across both philanthropic behaviors, engaged people were characterized by more adaptive personality trait levels (Bleidorn, Hopwood, Ackerman, et al., 2020; Pletzer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Across both philanthropic behaviors, engaged people were characterized by more adaptive personality trait levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Bleidorn, Hopwood, Ackerman, et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b143">Pletzer et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: One possible interpretation is that personality traits linked to individual functioning and thriving are associated with greater philanthropic engagement perhaps because they confer personal and social resources that facilitate such behaviors.

For example, traits such as extraversion and agreeableness are associated with larger and more active social networks and greater prosocial motivation, which may increase opportunities and willingness to engage (Bekkers, 2006; Okun et al., 2007).
text.formatted: For example, traits such as extraversion and agreeableness are associated with larger and more active social networks and greater prosocial motivation, which may increase opportunities and willingness to engage <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Bekkers, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">Okun et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, honesty-humility and openness/intellect may encompass values, such as broadmindedness, universalism, liberalism/non-authoritarianism, or benevolence (Desimoni & Leone, 2014; Dollinger et al., 1996; Fischer & Boer, 2015; Kajonius & Dåderman, 2014).
text.formatted: Similarly, honesty-humility and openness/intellect may encompass values, such as broadmindedness, universalism, liberalism/non-authoritarianism, or benevolence <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Desimoni & Leone, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Dollinger et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Fischer & Boer, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Kajonius & Dåderman, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Because these values reflect concern for community welfare beyond people's immediate close social circle, they may foster prosocial and civic engagement (Hilbig & Zettler, 2009; Mondak et al., 2010; Mondak & Halperin, 2008).
