text.text: personality differences should precede and predict subsequent engagement.
We examined this hypothesis prospectively.

The prospective pattern broadly mirrored concurrent findings: higher extraversion, higher openness/intellect, higher honesty-humility, and lower neuroticism emerged as predictors of both later volunteering and charitable giving.
These effects suggest that personality differences are not merely correlates of engagement but characterize who enters or maintains philanthropic behaviors over time.
Extraversion robustly predicted later volunteering, also when controlling for income, which likely reflects both motivation and opportunity (Funder, 2016; Rauthmann et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Extraversion robustly predicted later volunteering, also when controlling for income, which likely reflects both motivation and opportunity <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Funder, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">Rauthmann et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Extraverted individuals may perceive and encounter more opportunities to volunteer because they are socially integrated, have greater exposure to community initiatives, and may be more likely influenced by prosocially active peers (Okun et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Extraverted individuals may perceive and encounter more opportunities to volunteer because they are socially integrated, have greater exposure to community initiatives, and may be more likely influenced by prosocially active peers <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">(Okun et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, extraverted individuals may be more inclined to seek out philanthropic opportunities to fulfill their need for social reward and express agency (DeYoung et al., 2007; Kwon et al., 2023; Omoto et al., 2010).
text.formatted: At the same time, extraverted individuals may be more inclined to seek out philanthropic opportunities to fulfill their need for social reward and express agency <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(DeYoung et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">Kwon et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b139">Omoto et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Through repeated socially rewarding experiences, extraverted individuals may then also be more likely to sustain their engagement over time.
The less robust effect on charitable giving may reflect that donating is less rewarding for extraverts, as it is often done at a greater spatial and social distance (Kawawaki, 2023).
text.formatted: The less robust effect on charitable giving may reflect that donating is less rewarding for extraverts, as it is often done at a greater spatial and social distance <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">(Kawawaki, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: High openness/intellect may motivate people to engage with unfamiliar and diverse contexts in volunteer work (DeYoung et al., 2007).
text.formatted: High openness/intellect may motivate people to engage with unfamiliar and diverse contexts in volunteer work <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(DeYoung et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, this link did not hold once income was controlled, suggesting that openness/intellect's established link to higher income (Alderotti et al., 2023; Vella, 2024) may partly explain this prospective effect.
text.formatted: Notably, this link did not hold once income was controlled, suggesting that openness/intellect's established link to higher income <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alderotti et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b173">Vella, 2024</ref>) may partly explain this prospective effect.

text.text: In other words, people higher in openness/intellect may be more likely to take up or continue volunteering because they hold greater socioeconomic resources and thus have more flexibility in investing time in unpaid work.

We also found a selection effect of openness/intellect on later charitable giving, potentially reflecting people's higher awareness of societal needs (Bekkers & Wiepking, 2011) or attentiveness to political and social issues (Mondak et al., 2010; Mondak & Halperin, 2008).
text.formatted: We also found a selection effect of openness/intellect on later charitable giving, potentially reflecting people's higher awareness of societal needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Bekkers & Wiepking, 2011)</ref> or attentiveness to political and social issues <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">(Mondak et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Mondak & Halperin, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Honesty-humility was related to later charitable giving and to a lesser degree volunteering.
This is consistent with general expectations that this trait is related to prosocial behavior (Hilbig & Zettler, 2009; Smillie et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This is consistent with general expectations that this trait is related to prosocial behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Hilbig & Zettler, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">Smillie et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals low in this trait may be less likely to enter or sustain philanthropic engagement particularly in situations where it conflicts with selfish interests (Columbus et al., 2019; Zettler et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Individuals low in this trait may be less likely to enter or sustain philanthropic engagement particularly in situations where it conflicts with selfish interests <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Columbus et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b193">Zettler et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: It should also be noted that the honesty-humility scale includes items that refer to relative disinterest in personal wealth and material gain.
An alternative explanation is thus that there is overlap between the item content of the scale and prosocial outcomes that involve material sacrifice (e.g., Górnik-Durose & Pilch, 2016).
text.formatted: An alternative explanation is thus that there is overlap between the item content of the scale and prosocial outcomes that involve material sacrifice (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Górnik-Durose & Pilch, 2016</ref>).

text.text: An unexpected finding was the consistent association between neuroticism and philanthropic behavior, although associations with charitable giving were no longer significant when controlling for income.
This complements the broader notion that adaptive trait levels facilitate philanthropic engagement, and maladaptive trait levels may, in turn, hinder engagement.

Specifically, neurotic people may refrain or withdraw from philanthropic engagement due to lower perceived self-efficacy (Barańczuk, 2021; Bekkers & Wiepking, 2011) or reduced interpersonal trust (Chapman et al., 2021; Evans & Revelle, 2008; Thielmann et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Specifically, neurotic people may refrain or withdraw from philanthropic engagement due to lower perceived self-efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Barańczuk, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Bekkers & Wiepking, 2011)</ref> or reduced interpersonal trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Chapman et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Evans & Revelle, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b171">Thielmann et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, they may perceive volunteer work as more demanding or stressful, which could discourage them from engaging.
Although these prospective findings largely reinforced the importance of personality traits, they also diverged from the concurrent pattern in theoretically informative ways.
Most notably, agreeableness predicted subsequent charitable giving but not volunteering.

Although this finding contrasts with earlier theoretical accounts (e.g., Bekkers, 2006; Carlo et al., 2005), it aligns with recent meta-analytic evidence (Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025) and is consistent with the modest associations between volunteering and charitable giving observed in our sample.
text.formatted: Although this finding contrasts with earlier theoretical accounts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Bekkers, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Carlo et al., 2005)</ref>, it aligns with recent meta-analytic evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025)</ref> and is consistent with the modest associations between volunteering and charitable giving observed in our sample.

text.text: The divergence between theory and empirical data at the domain-level has also raised the possibility that broad agreeableness may be too heterogeneous to capture the specific motivational processes underlying philanthropic engagement and narrower aspects may diverge in meaningful ways (Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025; White et al., 2017; Yarkoni et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The divergence between theory and empirical data at the domain-level has also raised the possibility that broad agreeableness may be too heterogeneous to capture the specific motivational processes underlying philanthropic engagement and narrower aspects may diverge in meaningful ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Bleidorn, Stahlmann, Orth, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b176">White et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b190">Yarkoni et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Our analyses support this idea as compassion showed stronger and more consistent links to philanthropic engagement than politeness.
Compassion reflects affiliative emotions and empathy, whereas politeness captures more cognitive facets of agreeableness, such as respectfulness and fairness (DeYoung et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Compassion reflects affiliative emotions and empathy, whereas politeness captures more cognitive facets of agreeableness, such as respectfulness and fairness <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(DeYoung et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Affective tendencies may thus play a more important role in motivating philanthropic engagement than more abstract moral or normative considerations.

The link between compassion and charitable giving may, for example, reflect that agreeable people seek a "joy of giving" or act out of altruistic feelings when donating money rather than adhering to fairness norms (Bekkers & Wiepking, 2011; Zhao et al., 2017a).
text.formatted: The link between compassion and charitable giving may, for example, reflect that agreeable people seek a "joy of giving" or act out of altruistic feelings when donating money rather than adhering to fairness norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Bekkers & Wiepking, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zhao et al., 2017a)</ref>.

text.text: This reasoning aligns with research highlighting the role of concepts such as altruism, generosity, or empathy (Andreoni, 2006; Graziano et al., 2007), which resonate more closely with compassion rather than politeness.
text.formatted: This reasoning aligns with research highlighting the role of concepts such as altruism, generosity, or empathy <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Andreoni, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Graziano et al., 2007)</ref>, which resonate more closely with compassion rather than politeness.

text.text: A similar pattern emerged for prospective selection effects of conscientiousness aspects.
Orderliness, which partly reflects obligation to rules and norms, was unrelated to later philanthropic behavior, suggesting that moral standards alone may be less relevant to prosocial action.

Conversely, positive links between industriousness and volunteering and charitable giving may reflect industrious people's commitment and willingness to follow through on prosocial intentions (Ajzen et al., 2009; Wilmot & Ones, 2019).
text.formatted: Conversely, positive links between industriousness and volunteering and charitable giving may reflect industrious people's commitment and willingness to follow through on prosocial intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ajzen et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b178">Wilmot & Ones, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This contrasts with earlier accounts suggesting that ambition and dutifulness may hinder philanthropic engagement by prioritizing career advancement (Stahlmann et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This contrasts with earlier accounts suggesting that ambition and dutifulness may hinder philanthropic engagement by prioritizing career advancement <ref type="bibr" target="#b164">(Stahlmann et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings on differences between the two conscientiousness aspects suggest a more nuanced pattern, with industriousness promoting sustainment of philanthropy rather than hindering it.
These considerations illustrate how integrating personality effects at different levels can help reconcile previously inconclusive findings.

More broadly, these findings align with prior research highlighting the predictive validity of narrower personality traits (Jang et al., 2002; Mõttus et al., 2017; Stewart et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2018).
text.formatted: More broadly, these findings align with prior research highlighting the predictive validity of narrower personality traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Jang et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">Mõttus et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">Stewart et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b167">Sun et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the present findings suggest that understanding selection effects benefits from differentiated personality measures and longitudinal designs.
The latter also allow us to disentangle these selection effects from the socialization effect considered next.

Consistent with the social investment principle (Roberts et al., 2005; Roberts & Nickel, 2017), we expected that sustained involvement in volunteer work would be linked to personality development through psychologically meaningful experiences.
text.formatted: Consistent with the social investment principle <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">(Roberts et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b152">Roberts & Nickel, 2017)</ref>, we expected that sustained involvement in volunteer work would be linked to personality development through psychologically meaningful experiences.

text.text: Supporting this idea, socialization analyses indicated that, among engaged volunteers, people who spent more time volunteering on average showed a slightly less negative extraversion trajectory.
However, this effect did not hold when controlling for income.
This may reflect reduced power in the smaller subsample as the income-adjusted analyses included fewer participants.
Alternatively, income may partly account for the association between volunteering and extraversion change, or the inconsistent results may reflect sampling variability.
The socialization effect on extraversion should therefore be interpreted cautiously and requires replication.
Nevertheless, there are plausible mechanisms through which more intensive volunteering could contribute to greater stability in extraversion.
Highly engaged volunteers may be more likely to take on tasks involving responsibility, coordination, or leadership than people who spend less time volunteering.

For these people, volunteerism is more likely to constitute a meaningful, intrinsically motivated social role they identify with rather than a casual activity they pursue to pass their time (Lodi-Smith & Roberts, 2007; Luhmann et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For these people, volunteerism is more likely to constitute a meaningful, intrinsically motivated social role they identify with rather than a casual activity they pursue to pass their time <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Lodi-Smith & Roberts, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">Luhmann et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Such agentic and committed roles may foster positive affect and a sense of influence, which could, over time, consolidate into extraverted tendencies (Anderson et al., 2012; Ensari et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Such agentic and committed roles may foster positive affect and a sense of influence, which could, over time, consolidate into extraverted tendencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Anderson et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Ensari et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, volunteering may provide sustained opportunities for social interaction, particularly for people who are regularly engaged.

Given that social networks tend to shrink across adulthood (Wrzus et al., 2013), frequent volunteering may counteract this reduction in social contact and thereby contribute to more stable extraversion trajectories.
text.formatted: Given that social networks tend to shrink across adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b183">(Wrzus et al., 2013)</ref>, frequent volunteering may counteract this reduction in social contact and thereby contribute to more stable extraversion trajectories.

text.text: At the same time, the reverse direction cannot be ruled out: individuals with more stable trajectories of extraversion may also be more likely to sustain higher levels of volunteering, as continued social motivation and opportunity could support ongoing involvement.

Regardless of the direction, the observed pattern may be relevant for psychological well-being, given that both extraversion and sustained social participation have emerged as important correlates of mental health in prior meta-analytic research (Das et al., 2025; Hui et al., 2020; Pletzer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Regardless of the direction, the observed pattern may be relevant for psychological well-being, given that both extraversion and sustained social participation have emerged as important correlates of mental health in prior meta-analytic research <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Das et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Hui et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b143">Pletzer et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, no socialization effect emerged for honesty-humility and the other Big Five traits including openness/intellect, for which we had expected a positive volunteering effect.
This null finding may indicate that greater investment in volunteering among those already engaged does not provide sufficient novelty or cognitive stimulation to meaningfully shape this trait.

More generally, it adds to prior research suggesting that socialization effects on personality traits tend to be smaller and less consistent than selection effects (e.g., Andrae et al., 2026; Krämer et al., 2026; Nissen et al., 2022).
text.formatted: More generally, it adds to prior research suggesting that socialization effects on personality traits tend to be smaller and less consistent than selection effects (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Andrae et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Krämer et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Nissen et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The specificity of the one observed socialization effect may also be informative when comparing volunteering with charitable giving, for which we neither expected nor observed socialization effects.

Although both behaviors are grouped under the umbrella of traditional philanthropy (Bekkers, 2006), volunteering may be more likely to shape personality trajectories because it typically involves more intensive time investment, role obligations, and coordination with others.
text.formatted: Although both behaviors are grouped under the umbrella of traditional philanthropy <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Bekkers, 2006)</ref>, volunteering may be more likely to shape personality trajectories because it typically involves more intensive time investment, role obligations, and coordination with others.

text.text: Charitable giving, in contrast, can often be enacted at greater social and physical distance from recipients and the concrete context of need (Kawawaki, 2023).
text.formatted: Charitable giving, in contrast, can often be enacted at greater social and physical distance from recipients and the concrete context of need <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">(Kawawaki, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, even if donating time and money can serve related psychological functions (Andreoni, 2006; Choi & Kim, 2011; Johnson & Park, 2021) and tend to be empirically linked (Hill, 2012; Wiepking & Maas, 2009), they may differ in their potential to provide the sustained social-role experiences through which personality development is expected to occur.
text.formatted: Thus, even if donating time and money can serve related psychological functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Andreoni, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Choi & Kim, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Johnson & Park, 2021)</ref> and tend to be empirically linked <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">(Hill, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b177">Wiepking & Maas, 2009)</ref>, they may differ in their potential to provide the sustained social-role experiences through which personality development is expected to occur.

text.text: However, we did not test this difference directly.
In sum, volunteering and charitable giving may be partially overlapping but psychologically distinct forms of philanthropy.
Beyond this distinction between forms of engagement, age-graded changes in resources, opportunities, and role demands may also shape personality-philanthropy transactions.
This lifespan perspective guided our final set of analyses.
Across analyses, age moderation effects were inconsistent and very small in magnitude.
The most consistent pattern emerged for agreeableness and its aspect compassion: Associations with philanthropic engagement tended to increase slightly with age.
In particular, prospective selection effects of compassion on subsequent engagement were stronger at older ages, even when controlling for income.

A possible interpretation is that dispositional differences in compassion become more consequential for behavioral choices later in life, when competing role demands tend to decline and people have greater flexibility to engage in activities aligned with their traits (Blum et al., 2018).
text.formatted: A possible interpretation is that dispositional differences in compassion become more consequential for behavioral choices later in life, when competing role demands tend to decline and people have greater flexibility to engage in activities aligned with their traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Blum et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, age-related increases in generativity and prosocial values may amplify the behavioral expression of compassionate dispositions in older adulthood (Fung et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Alternatively, age-related increases in generativity and prosocial values may amplify the behavioral expression of compassionate dispositions in older adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Fung et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Apart from this pattern, the largely absent and inconsistent age moderation effects suggest that associations between personality traits and philanthropic engagement are relatively stable across the adult lifespan.

This pattern might indicate that the mechanisms linking personality traits and philanthropic engagement-such as social motivation, compassion, or value-driven behavior-may operate similarly across different life stages despite changing external constraints.
However, the absence of robust moderation should be interpreted cautiously.
Given the generally small effect sizes, statistical power to detect even smaller interaction effects may have been limited.

Moreover, chronological age may be too coarse to capture meaningful life-stage differences, as more proximal factors such as retirement, health, or time availability may better reflect changes in opportunity structures for engagement (Komp et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Moreover, chronological age may be too coarse to capture meaningful life-stage differences, as more proximal factors such as retirement, health, or time availability may better reflect changes in opportunity structures for engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Komp et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: It is possible that selection into philanthropic activities occurs earlier in life, leaving less room for age-differentiated effects in later adulthood.

Given these constraints and the exploratory nature of our analyses, future research should examine more specific life transitions and employ fine-grained longitudinal designs to better understand potential agedependent processes in personality-philanthropy transactions.
The present findings have several theoretical and practical implications.
From a theoretical perspective, this study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of the associations between personality traits and philanthropy.

Personality traits primarily emerged as characteristics that concurrently and prospectively predict individual differences in philanthropic engagement and to a lesser degree as personal tendencies that might be shaped through sustained interactions with one's social environment.

Similarly, philanthropic activities are not only behavioral endpoints predicted by personality, but also potentially psychologically consequential experiences that can relate to personality development over time.

This adds to a broader body of literature emphasizing the transactional relations between personality and social contexts (Neyer et al., 2014; Wrzus et al., 2016), which at the same time suggests that selection processes tend to be more pronounced than socialization processes (e.g., E. Beck, 2019).

Beck, 2019).

text.text: Our use of both broad personality domains and narrower aspects speaks to a long-standing tension between breadth and precision in personality science (Paunonen & Ashton, 2001; Wittmann & Süß, 1999).

text.text: Trait hierarchies address this tension by capturing the major dimensions of individual differences at multiple levels of abstraction, from broad domains to narrower aspects and facets (e.g., DeYoung et al., 2007; Soto & John, 2017).

text.text: In line with prior research (e.g., Stewart et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2018), our aspect-level findings showed that narrower traits can contribute to a more nuanced understanding of philanthropic behavior beyond broad domains alone.

text.text: Meta-analytic associations between constructs like moral identity and moral behaviors (r = .20; Hertz & Krettenauer, 2016), volunteer-related values and frequency of volunteering (r = .17; Zhou & Kodama Muscente, 2023), and social identification and charitable giving (r = .29; Chapman et al., 2025) are often stronger than those observed for personality traits.
text.formatted: Meta-analytic associations between constructs like moral identity and moral behaviors (r = .20; <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Hertz & Krettenauer, 2016)</ref>, volunteer-related values and frequency of volunteering (r = .17; <ref type="bibr" target="#b198">Zhou & Kodama Muscente, 2023)</ref>, and social identification and charitable giving (r = .29; <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Chapman et al., 2025)</ref> are often stronger than those observed for personality traits.

text.text: This raises questions about how to understand these kinds of variables from a personality perspective.

Although it has been argued that constructs such as moral foundations represent unique content that is not captured by personality (Feher & Vernon, 2021; Haidt et al., 2009), it is also possible that these associations reflect predictor specificity within a general model of individual differences.
text.formatted: Although it has been argued that constructs such as moral foundations represent unique content that is not captured by personality <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Feher & Vernon, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Haidt et al., 2009)</ref>, it is also possible that these associations reflect predictor specificity within a general model of individual differences.

text.text: Attitudes toward volunteering, for example, are more closely aligned with volunteering behavior than broad patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, but this does not necessarily mean that such variables cannot be considered a part of personality traits writ large.

From a lexical perspective, Big Five and HEXACO dimensions are theorized to comprehensively cover individual differences in non-cognitive, normal range psychological functioning (Ashton & Lee, 2007; Goldberg, 1993; John & Srivastava, 1999).
text.formatted: From a lexical perspective, Big Five and HEXACO dimensions are theorized to comprehensively cover individual differences in non-cognitive, normal range psychological functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Ashton & Lee, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Goldberg, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">John & Srivastava, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: There is indeed reliable evidence that values, moral identity, or political ideology are systematically related to Big Five and HEXACO variables (Fischer & Boer, 2015; Hirsh et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2021), as are constructs designed to extend beyond these frameworks (Lee et al., 2005).
text.formatted: There is indeed reliable evidence that values, moral identity, or political ideology are systematically related to Big Five and HEXACO variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Fischer & Boer, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Hirsh et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b187">Xu et al., 2021)</ref>, as are constructs designed to extend beyond these frameworks <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">(Lee et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: While it is not surprising that predictive power improves the more similar the item content of a scale is to the predicted outcome, we would maintain that broad personality frameworks provide a useful framework for understanding the broader network of correlates of philanthropic engagement (Anglim & O'Connor, 2019).
text.formatted: While it is not surprising that predictive power improves the more similar the item content of a scale is to the predicted outcome, we would maintain that broad personality frameworks provide a useful framework for understanding the broader network of correlates of philanthropic engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Anglim & O'Connor, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: From an applied perspective, our findings could inform efforts to promote philanthropic engagement.

Solicitations could be tailored to personality-relevant motivations, for example by emphasizing socially rewarding aspects, highlighting opportunities for learning and novel experiences, or framing appeals in terms of compassion (Bekkers & Wiepking, 2011; Hirsh et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Solicitations could be tailored to personality-relevant motivations, for example by emphasizing socially rewarding aspects, highlighting opportunities for learning and novel experiences, or framing appeals in terms of compassion <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Bekkers & Wiepking, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Hirsh et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, personality-informed outreach strategies could also be used to broaden participation by designing appeals and opportunities that resonate with individuals less inclined toward volunteering or donating.

For example, people lower in extraversion may be more responsive to low-social-intensity forms of volunteering, whereas donation appeals for people higher in neuroticism may benefit from reducing uncertainty, emphasizing clear impact, and providing reassurance about trustworthiness of the organization.

Importantly, implementing such targeted approaches both ethically and effectively will require transparency and collaboration with engaged communities to foster agency, trust, and sustainable involvement (Matz et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Importantly, implementing such targeted approaches both ethically and effectively will require transparency and collaboration with engaged communities to foster agency, trust, and sustainable involvement <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">(Matz et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, our findings speak to the policy relevance of personality traits (Bleidorn et al., 2019) and align with prior research showing mutual links between prosociality, personality, and individual well-being (Hui et al., 2020; Smillie et al., 2019; Thielmann et al., 2020).
text.formatted: More broadly, our findings speak to the policy relevance of personality traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Bleidorn et al., 2019)</ref> and align with prior research showing mutual links between prosociality, personality, and individual well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">(Hui et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">Smillie et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b171">Thielmann et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This policy relevance should be interpreted cautiously, however, given the small size of the observed effects.

Rather than suggesting that personality traits strongly predict any single person's philanthropic behavior, the findings point to the potential value of broad, sustained, and low-cost approaches that may shift engagement patterns at the population level.

Accordingly, interventions that foster wellbeing, prosocial activities, or adaptive personality functioning may be most consequential when evaluated in terms of cumulative population-level impact rather than large individual-level change.
This study has several important limitations.

First, although the longitudinal design improves on cross-sectional approaches by establishing temporal ordering and allowing us to distinguish withinfrom between-person variation, the observational nature of the data precludes causal conclusions.
The findings are consistent with selection and socialization processes, but time-varying within-person confounders cannot be ruled out.
For example, changes in health or family responsibilities may simultaneously shape personality development and opportunities for philanthropic engagement.

Future research could move closer to causal inference by specifying the broader causal network of these associations more explicitly and, where feasible, combining repeated assessments of theoretically relevant contextual changes with longitudinal causal inference approaches (Chatton & Rohrer, 2024; Loh & Ren, 2023).
text.formatted: Future research could move closer to causal inference by specifying the broader causal network of these associations more explicitly and, where feasible, combining repeated assessments of theoretically relevant contextual changes with longitudinal causal inference approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Chatton & Rohrer, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">Loh & Ren, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Complementary quasi-experimental or intervention-based designs, such as programs that facilitate volunteering or encourage charitable giving, would provide further evidence.
Second, the 2-year observation period may have limited our ability to capture long-term personality development.
Personality change often unfolds gradually and may be difficult to detect reliably across relatively short intervals (Jackson & Wright, 2024).
text.formatted: Personality change often unfolds gradually and may be difficult to detect reliably across relatively short intervals <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Jackson & Wright, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, a previous examination in this sample found comparatively high rank-order stability of personality domains and aspects (Haehner, Krämer, Schaefer, et al., 2026), suggesting that the present window may be too short to detect longer-term personality-philanthropy transactions.
text.formatted: Relatedly, a previous examination in this sample found comparatively high rank-order stability of personality domains and aspects <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Haehner, Krämer, Schaefer, et al., 2026)</ref>, suggesting that the present window may be too short to detect longer-term personality-philanthropy transactions.

text.text: At the same time, personality traits can change within several months (Bleidorn, 2012; Wright et al., 2026), and the present 6-month schedule is more sensitive to such short-term change than panel studies with multi-year intervals (Bleidorn, Hopwood, Back, et al., 2020; Luhmann et al., 2014).
text.formatted: At the same time, personality traits can change within several months <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Bleidorn, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b181">Wright et al., 2026)</ref>, and the present 6-month schedule is more sensitive to such short-term change than panel studies with multi-year intervals <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Bleidorn, Hopwood, Back, et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">Luhmann et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should therefore examine these processes with longer study durations while maintaining relatively frequent assessments to capture both long-term developmental trajectories and short-term change in personality and philanthropy simultaneously across time (Roemer et al., 2025; Wrzus & Roberts, 2017).
text.formatted: Future research should therefore examine these processes with longer study durations while maintaining relatively frequent assessments to capture both long-term developmental trajectories and short-term change in personality and philanthropy simultaneously across time <ref type="bibr" target="#b155">(Roemer et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b185">Wrzus & Roberts, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Third, both personality traits and philanthropic behaviors were assessed via self-report.

Selfreports of personality traits can be constrained by imperfect self-insight and socially desirable responding (Grimm, 2010; Ziegler et al., 2010), which may have led people to report more adaptive personality levels such as high agreeableness or low neuroticism (Bleidorn, Hopwood, Ackerman, et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Selfreports of personality traits can be constrained by imperfect self-insight and socially desirable responding <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Grimm, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b199">Ziegler et al., 2010)</ref>, which may have led people to report more adaptive personality levels such as high agreeableness or low neuroticism <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Bleidorn, Hopwood, Ackerman, et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A multi-method approach additionally integrating, for example, informant ratings or observational data could provide more comprehensive and predictive information on personality in future studies (e.g., Connolly et al., 2007; Mõttus & Henry, 2025; Roberts, Harms, et al., 2006).
text.formatted: A multi-method approach additionally integrating, for example, informant ratings or observational data could provide more comprehensive and predictive information on personality in future studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Connolly et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">Mõttus & Henry, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">Roberts, Harms, et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, distortion of philanthropic measures through socially desirable responding is probably lower, because items assessing concrete, recent behaviors rely more on direct recall than on abstract selfevaluation and inflating one's responses would require misreporting actual behavior rather than interpreting one's traits favorably.
However, self-reported philanthropic behavior is vulnerable to recall error, particularly estimates of volunteering time and donation amounts.
In addition, the philanthropy measures were rather coarse.

They provide useful indicators of overall charitable giving and volunteering but do not distinguish between various activities, goals, or motives of philanthropy (Ackermann, 2019; A. Farmer et al., 2020; Nilsson et al., 2020).
text.formatted: They provide useful indicators of overall charitable giving and volunteering but do not distinguish between various activities, goals, or motives of philanthropy <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ackermann, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">A. Farmer et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">Nilsson et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth and relatedly, associations may partly reflect shared method variance rather than solely substantive links between personality and philanthropic engagement (Podsakoff et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Fourth and relatedly, associations may partly reflect shared method variance rather than solely substantive links between personality and philanthropic engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">(Podsakoff et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: General response tendencies, current mood, or the situational context may have jointly distorted responses of both personality and philanthropy variables, thereby inflating associations.
However, if such biases were driving results, associations should be inflated fairly uniformly across traits and engagement indicators, yet we observed substantial variability across associations.
Moreover, repeated, temporally separated assessments in longitudinal analyses are unlikely to be systematically affected by transient situational influences (Podsakoff et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Moreover, repeated, temporally separated assessments in longitudinal analyses are unlikely to be systematically affected by transient situational influences <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">(Podsakoff et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, predictors and outcome variables had little semantic overlap, and recall of concrete behavior should be less susceptible to shared method variance than, for example, self-reported intentions (Baumsteiger & Siegel, 2019) or behavioral motives (Zhou & Kodama Muscente, 2023).
text.formatted: Finally, predictors and outcome variables had little semantic overlap, and recall of concrete behavior should be less susceptible to shared method variance than, for example, self-reported intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Baumsteiger & Siegel, 2019)</ref> or behavioral motives <ref type="bibr" target="#b198">(Zhou & Kodama Muscente, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should nonetheless complement self-reports with objective behavioral records, such as register-based donation data (Elinder & Erixson, 2025), which eliminate shared method variance by design and may also help differentiate different philanthropic causes (such as donations to local versus international institutions).
text.formatted: Future studies should nonetheless complement self-reports with objective behavioral records, such as register-based donation data <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Elinder & Erixson, 2025)</ref>, which eliminate shared method variance by design and may also help differentiate different philanthropic causes (such as donations to local versus international institutions).

text.text: Finally, the present data support generalizability to the Swiss context but only to a limited extent beyond it.

Levels of philanthropic engagement are relatively high in Switzerland compared to rates in other European countries (Eurostat, 2024) and worldwide (Nakamura, Gibson, et al., 2025; Nakamura, Węziak-Białowolska, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Levels of philanthropic engagement are relatively high in Switzerland compared to rates in other European countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Eurostat, 2024)</ref> and worldwide <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">(Nakamura, Gibson, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">Nakamura, Węziak-Białowolska, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Official Swiss statistics find that 39.2% of the population report having engaged in volunteering in the past 4 weeks (21.3% institutionalized, 26.3% informal; Bundesamt für Statistik, 2021) and that 82% of Swiss households donated money to charitable causes in 2024 (Swissfundraising & Stiftung Zewo, 2025).
text.formatted: Official Swiss statistics find that 39.2% of the population report having engaged in volunteering in the past 4 weeks (21.3% institutionalized, 26.3% informal; Bundesamt für Statistik, 2021) and that 82% of Swiss households donated money to charitable causes in 2024 <ref type="bibr" target="#b168">(Swissfundraising & Stiftung Zewo, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These figures are broadly comparable to our 6-month prevalences in volunteering (35.7-39.0% vs. a 4-week benchmark) and charitable giving (64.4-74.2% vs. an annual household benchmark) and do not indicate systematic over-reporting.
At the same time, high lifetime prevalences, particularly for charitable giving (92%), leave little variance to be explained and may have limited the size of associations.

These high levels of engagement potentially reflect context-specific features of Switzerland such as a dense network of civic organizations, high wealth, or a strong humanitarian tradition (Bauer et al., 2013).
text.formatted: These high levels of engagement potentially reflect context-specific features of Switzerland such as a dense network of civic organizations, high wealth, or a strong humanitarian tradition <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Bauer et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Such contextspecificities as well as cross-cultural variation in developmental trajectories of personality traits may alter personality-philanthropy links across countries and cultures (Thalmayer et al., 2022; Uskul et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Such contextspecificities as well as cross-cultural variation in developmental trajectories of personality traits may alter personality-philanthropy links across countries and cultures <ref type="bibr" target="#b169">(Thalmayer et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b172">Uskul et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should therefore examine associations between personality traits and philanthropy across different cultural contexts.
This study provides a longitudinal perspective on the associations between personality traits and philanthropic engagement.

Across concurrent and prospective analyses, higher extraversion and lower neuroticism showed consistent links with volunteering, whereas agreeableness and honestyhumility were robustly associated with charitable giving.

At the more fine-grained aspect level, compassion and industriousness emerged as important aspects in prospectively predicting philanthropic behaviors whereas politeness and orderliness were largely unrelated to later philanthropic engagement.
Beyond these selection effects, people who spent more time volunteering on average showed less negative extraversion development over time.

Although this effect was very small and not robust across analyses, it provides initial evidence that philanthropic engagement may not only reflect personality differences but could also relate to personality change.
Overall, these findings suggest that targeted solicitation and outreach strategies could leverage personality-relevant motives to promote volunteering and charitable giving in real-world contexts.

At the same time, future research should use more rigorous causal designs and longer-term multi-method assessments to better understand when and how personality and philanthropy shape one another across the lifespan.
